big_idea: We can READ code and predict what it will do BEFORE running it. Predicting tests our understanding.
learning_intention: We are learning to read code and predict what will happen when it runs.
student_learning_goal: I can read code and predict what will happen when it runs.
success_criteria: I can read a piece of code with sequential steps.
I can predict where the robot will end before running.
I can predict the outcome of code that includes a loop.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Coda the Coding Robot — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Per-pair set of existing code sample cards (12)
Lesson 3 prediction tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Coda gives you code BEFORE running. Can you PREDICT where Coda will end up? Coda opens: 'PREDICT then CHECK — that's how we read code!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Day 1 we WROTE step-by-step code with Coda. Day 2 Looper showed us LOOPS. Today we READ code Coda hands us. Tomorrow we'll ALTER it.

Bring children to the carpet. Reveal Coda. 'Friends — yesterday we WROTE code. Today Coda gives us code that's ALREADY WRITTEN. Our job is to READ it and PREDICT what happens.'

Show code on the chart:
Step 1: right
Step 2: right
Step 3: up
Step 4: right

Start Coda at (0,0) on the grid. 'Coda STARTS HERE. Where will Coda END UP after this code? PREDICT first.'

Give children 30 seconds to think. Take predictions: '(3, 1)' or 'three squares right and one up'. 'OK — let's check.' Move Coda step by step. Land at (3, 1). 'PREDICTION CORRECT.'

Now harder code with a loop:
Repeat 3: right
Up
Repeat 2: right

'Predict?' Children think: 3 rights = (3,0). Then up = (3,1). Then 2 rights = (5,1). 'Predict (5, 1).' Run: Coda lands at (5, 1). 'CORRECT.'

'Today we'll READ lots of code and PREDICT outcomes. Then we'll RUN to check.'
student_actions: Predict the ending square BEFORE running.

steps.instruction: Whole group: predict outcomes for 3 more codes. (a) right, right, up, up, right (3,2). (b) Repeat 4: right (4,0). (c) Repeat 2: right, up (2,2). For each, predict first, run second.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three codes. PREDICT first. Then we run.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Predict-Check Cards — pair has 6 code cards; predict ending square, then run to verify. Station B: Predict the SHAPE — pair has 4 code cards that draw shapes (square, triangle, etc.); predict the shape, then trace. Station C: Two-Step Predict — pair has 4 codes that include 'turn' commands; predict ending position AND direction.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include 2 codes with NESTED loops or longer sequences. Predict carefully.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs: 'Some codes are tricky — read each line carefully.'

steps.instruction: Discuss when predictions go wrong. 'If you predict wrong, what does that tell you?' Lead to: 'Maybe I missed a step. Maybe I miscounted. Predicting wrong is OK — it helps us LEARN.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Normalise wrong predictions. They're how we discover misreadings.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the prediction tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'What's your prediction? Why?' before running. Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: 'How did YOU predict Coda's destination?' Some children traced on paper; some pictured Coda walking; some used a finger on the grid. Pairs share strategies and decide: which is fastest? Which is most accurate for long codes (10+ steps with loops)? Battista (2007) names path-tracing strategies as the core of spatial-reasoning literacy.
steps.teacher_prompt: Coda: 'Different brains, different paths to the same answer. Try one strategy today, try another tomorrow — find what works for YOUR brain.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use 3-step codes only.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: codes with 8+ steps or 2 loops.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide step-by-step prediction frame: 'After step 1, Coda is at ___. After step 2, Coda is at ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Allow them to walk Coda's path on a floor grid — body-on-grid predicting.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: predicts ending position correctly; predicts shape from code; explains the prediction.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the prediction tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: What does it mean to PREDICT?
How do you predict where Coda ends up?
What happens when your prediction is wrong?
How does predicting help you understand code?
Tomorrow we'll ALTER Coda's code (Lesson 4 — C3.2). If today you predicted Coda lands on (3,2), what would you change to make him land on (4,2) instead? That's tomorrow's question.
consolidation.exit_routine: Coda's refrain — class chants together: "PREDICT then CHECK — that's how we read code!" Then call-and-response with Looper: 'Loops make it SHORT!' Each child writes their PREDICT square on a sticky and CHECKs by tracing on the carpet grid.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child predicts the ending position by JUST counting steps without considering direction — repairing the direction-blind prediction
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
When children READ code (rather than write it), Grade 1's main trap is losing position-track on a grid — they correctly read each command (forward, turn right) but lose where Coda is, especially after loops execute. Battista (2007) 'The Development of Geometric and Spatial Thinking' frames this as path-and-position memory; Clements & Sarama (2009) place coordinated tracking of direction + position in the early-childhood spatial trajectory.

Day 1 we WROTE step-by-step code with Coda. Day 2 Looper showed us LOOPS. Today we READ code Coda hands us. Tomorrow we'll ALTER it. Today's predict-and-check work consolidates Days 1-2 spatial literacy.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Code: right, up, right, up, right. Child predicts 'Coda moved 5 steps'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Tell me where Coda ENDS UP, not how many steps.' The child looks puzzled. 'Walk through each step. Step 1: right — Coda goes from (0,0) to (1,0). Step 2: up — Coda goes from (1,0) to (1,1). Continue.'

Walk together: (0,0) → (1,0) → (1,1) → (2,1) → (2,2) → (3,2). 'Coda ends at (3, 2).' Tick the tracker.

'Direction matters. Each step changes WHICH WAY Coda goes. Predict ending position, not just step count.'

Long-term recovery: trace each step on paper before predicting. Build the direction-aware reflex.
expected_student_responses: (Strong) Traces each step's effect on position.
(Stretched) Predicts shape AND ending position together.
common_misconceptions: All steps are the same. (Repair: each step's direction matters.)
Counting steps = predicting position. (Repair: position = sum of directions.)
Loops always go right. (Repair: the loop body determines direction — could be 'up, up' or any other.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child reads steps but loses position: paper-trace — child puts finger on grid start, says command aloud, MOVES finger physically before next command.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child cannot name 'right'/'up' as directions: stand the child up, name body-relative directions ('your right hand'), then transfer to grid with arrow stickers as anchors.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child correctly tracks position but cannot predict loops: unroll the loop on paper ('Repeat 3' = write the inside 3 times underneath), then re-read.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C3.2 (read code and predict).

parts_outline.task: Read 6 code samples; predict ending position on the grid.
Read 4 code samples that draw shapes; predict the shape.
Open prompt: read this code with a loop and predict.
